title: Project Setup & Deck Model
summary: Start from zero: install Godot 4.3, create the Kadi project and tour the editor, write your first script on a node — then lay the project's skeleton: enums for suits and ranks, custom Resources for card data, a deck builder using nested loops, and Autoloads for shared game state.

lessons.title: Installing Godot 4.3
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Installing Godot 4.3

Before a single card hits the table, we need the tool we will build Kadi with: **Godot 4.3**, a free, open-source game engine. Download it from the official site, [godotengine.org](https://godotengine.org) — never from third-party mirrors, which may bundle outdated or tampered builds.

On the download page you will see two builds: **Standard** and **.NET**. The .NET build adds C# support; the Standard build ships GDScript, Godot's own Python-like language. Kadi is written entirely in GDScript, so choose **Standard**. Pick the version matching your OS — Windows, macOS, or Linux are all first-class citizens.

Here is the surprise: there is **no installer**. Godot is a single portable executable around 100 MB. Unzip it anywhere — your Desktop, a `tools` folder, a USB stick — and double-click. Nothing is written to the registry; deleting the file uninstalls it completely.

```gdscript
# Once Godot is running, this is the kind of code we will write:
func _ready() -> void:
    print("Godot 4.3 ready — time to build Kadi!")
```

On first launch you land in the **Project Manager** — a window listing your projects (empty for now) with buttons to create, import, or scan for projects. This is Godot's front door; the editor itself opens only after you pick a project.

> [!WHY]
> We pin the exact version — 4.3 Standard — because engine versions change APIs. A tutorial written for 4.3 (`instantiate()`, `@onready`, typed signals) will confuse you on 3.x, where those are spelled differently. Locking the version now means every snippet in this course runs exactly as printed, so any error you see is a learning moment, not a version mismatch.

With the Project Manager open, you are ready to create the Kadi project — that is the next lesson.

lessons.title: Creating the Kadi Project & Editor Tour
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Creating the Kadi Project

In the Project Manager click **New Project**. Name it `Kadi`, pick an empty folder (Godot fills it with the project files), and choose a **renderer**. Godot 4.3 offers **Forward+** (desktop-class 3D lighting) and **Compatibility** (runs everywhere, including old GPUs and the web). Kadi is a 2D card game with zero fancy lighting — choose **Compatibility**. You can switch later without losing work.

Click **Create & Edit** and the full editor opens. It looks busy at first; there are really only five regions to learn. The **Scene dock** (top-left) shows the tree of nodes in the currently open scene. The **FileSystem dock** (bottom-left) lists every file in your project folder — scripts, scenes, art — rooted at `res://`. The **Inspector** (right) shows every property of whatever node you select: position, texture, custom exported variables.

The centre is the **main viewport**, where you see and arrange your game visually. Along the bottom sits the **bottom panel** with tabs like **Output** (where `print()` text appears) and **Debugger** (errors and breakpoints). You will live in Output constantly while building Kadi's rules.

```gdscript
# Everything in the FileSystem dock is addressed with res:// paths:
const CARD_SCENE_PATH := "res://card/CardScene.tscn"
const CARD_BACK_ART := "res://art/card_back.png"
```

Press **F5** to run the project. The first time, Godot asks you to pick a **main scene** — the scene that boots when the game starts. Once you save a scene (next lesson) you can select it here, or set it later in **Project Settings → Application → Run → Main Scene**.

> [!WHY]
> Choosing Compatibility over Forward+ is not just simplicity — it is reach. Kadi should run on the aging laptop in a Nairobi cyber café as smoothly as on a gaming rig, and Compatibility's OpenGL backend guarantees that, plus effortless web export for sharing the game with friends. Forward+ buys advanced 3D lighting a flat card table will never use.

Spend two minutes clicking each dock now. Knowing where the Scene dock, Inspector, and Output live will save you hours across this course.

lessons.title: Nodes, Scenes, and Your First Script
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Nodes, Scenes, and Your First Script

Everything in Godot is a **node**: a sprite is a node, a label is a node, a sound player is a node. Nodes nest into a **tree** — a card node might contain a sprite node for its art and a label node for its rank. A **scene** is simply a tree of nodes saved to a `.tscn` file, and a **script** (`.gd` file) is behaviour you attach to a node.

Let's build the root of Kadi. In the Scene dock click **Other Node**, search for `Node2D` (the basic 2D node with a position), and create it. Double-click its name and rename it to `Main`. Press **Ctrl+S** to save the scene as `main.tscn` — this is the tree the whole game will hang from.

Now give it behaviour. With `Main` selected, click the **attach-script button** (the scroll-with-a-plus icon at the top of the Scene dock). Accept the defaults — `main.gd`, extending `Node2D` — and the script editor opens. Add a `_ready()` function, which Godot calls once when the node enters the running scene tree:

```gdscript
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
    print("Karibu Kadi!")
```

Press **F5**, choose `main.tscn` as the main scene when asked, and watch the **Output** tab: `Karibu Kadi!` — welcome to Kadi. That one line proves the whole pipeline works: scene loads, node enters the tree, script runs.

> [!WHY]
> Scene = saved tree of nodes (`.tscn`); script = behaviour attached to a node (`.gd`). Keeping structure and behaviour separate is Godot's core design: the same Card scene can carry different scripts (a face-up playable card versus a face-down opponent card), and the same script can drive many scenes. Every Kadi feature from here on — the deck, hands, the discard pile — is just nodes in trees with scripts attached.

From now on, when a lesson says "create a scene" or "attach a script", this is exactly the workflow: add node, rename, attach script, save, F5, read Output.

codeSnippets.caption: main.gd — your first script, attached to the Main (Node2D) root.

practicePrompt.instructions: Extend main.gd so _ready() also prints the number of players (a typed int variable `player_count` set to 4) using string formatting.
practicePrompt.hint: Declare `var player_count: int = 4` and use `%d` with the `%` operator inside print().
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
extends Node2D

var player_count: int = 4

func _ready() -> void:
    print("Karibu Kadi!")
    print("Players at the table: %d" % player_count)

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the relationship between a scene and a script in Godot?
choices: A scene is a saved tree of nodes (.tscn); a script is behaviour attached to a node (.gd)
quizQuestions.explanation: Scenes store structure (which nodes, how nested); scripts store behaviour. A node in a scene may or may not carry a script.

quizQuestions.prompt: When does Godot call the `_ready()` function on your Main node?
choices: Once, when the node enters the running scene tree
Only when you click the node
quizQuestions.explanation: `_ready()` fires once when the node (and its children) are in the tree — the perfect place for setup like printing a greeting or, later, dealing cards.

lessons.title: Enums for Suits and Ranks
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Enums

An **enum** (enumeration) is a set of named integer constants. In Kadi every suit and rank has a fixed identity — perfect for an enum.

```gdscript
class_name CardTypes
extends RefCounted

enum Suits { HEARTS, DIAMONDS, CLUBS, SPADES }
enum Ranks {
    TWO = 2, THREE, FOUR, FIVE, SIX, SEVEN, EIGHT, NINE, TEN,
    JACK = 11, QUEEN = 12, KING = 13, ACE = 14, JOKER = 15
}
```

By default enums count up from 0, but you can assign explicit values. Here we map rank values to their card face value so a 7 is 7, not 5. This single choice lets us reuse integers across the whole game: penalty math, sorting, comparison.

Access an enum member as `CardTypes.Ranks.ACE`. Use them everywhere instead of magic numbers — `card.rank == Ranks.JOKER` reads itself; `card.rank == 15` does not.

> [!WHY]
> Enums replace magic numbers with names. When you later add a new special card — say a custom "Wizard" rank — you add one enum entry and the compiler flags every place you forgot to handle it (with a `match` statement). Magic numbers give you no such safety net.

Keep enums in their own `class_name` script so other files import them as `CardTypes.Ranks.ACE` without preload gymnastics.

codeSnippets.caption: Enum definitions for suits and ranks, anchored at real card values.

practicePrompt.instructions: Add a new enum `CardKind` with values PENALTY, QUESTION, ANSWER, JUMP, KICKBACK, NORMAL, and write a function `is_special(kind)` returning true for everything except NORMAL.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why anchor Ranks at explicit values like TWO = 2 instead of letting them auto-increment from 0?
choices: So the integer equals the card's face value, simplifying penalty and comparison logic
quizQuestions.explanation: Aligning enum values with card face values means rank 7 IS the 7 of any suit — no lookup table needed for math.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do you reference the ACE member of the Ranks enum declared in `class_name CardTypes`?
quizQuestions.explanation: Fully-qualified enum access is `ClassName.EnumName.MEMBER`, ensuring no collision with other enums named Ranks.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does the `@export` annotation do to a Resource field?
choices: Exposes it to the Inspector so designers can edit it on .tres files
quizQuestions.explanation: `@export` surfaces the field in the editor, enabling data-driven design without touching code.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why use a Resource rather than a Dictionary for card data?
choices: Resources are reference-counted, inspectable, and savable to .tres files for designer editing
quizQuestions.explanation: Resources integrate with the editor and asset pipeline; dictionaries are just runtime structures with no Inspector support.

lessons.title: Building the Deck with Nested Loops
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Deck Builder

A standard Kadi deck is 52 cards (4 suits × 13 ranks) plus two Jokers. The cleanest way to generate it is a nested `for` loop: outer loop over suits, inner loop over ranks.

```gdscript
func build_deck() -> Array:
    var deck: Array = []
    for suit in range(4):
        for rank in range(2, 15):  # 2 through Ace (14)
            deck.append(CardData.make(suit, rank))
    deck.append(CardData.make(0, 15))  # Joker 1
    deck.append(CardData.make(1, 15))  # Joker 2
    return deck
```

`range(2, 15)` yields 2, 3, ..., 14 — the 13 ranks. We add the two Jokers manually because they have no suit constraint (we tag them with placeholder suits).

After building, **shuffle** the deck with `deck.shuffle()` (a Godot built-in that randomises in place). Shuffling uses a Fisher-Yates algorithm; results differ each run unless you seed the RNG.

> [!WHY]
> Generating the deck programmatically guarantees 52 unique cards every time. Hard-coding 52 literals would invite typos — a missing 7 of Clubs breaks the game silently. A nested loop is also self-documenting: read it and you see exactly the deck composition.

If you add a variant deck (e.g. two-pack Kadi), one constant change — `range(2, 15)` to two iterations — extends the builder.

codeSnippets.caption: Nested for loops build and shuffle a 54-card Kadi deck.

practicePrompt.instructions: Modify build_deck to build only the red suits (Hearts=0, Diamonds=1) for a mini-deck variant.
practicePrompt.hint: Change the outer range to only cover suits 0 and 1.

quizQuestions.explanation: Godot's `range(start, end)` is half-open: it includes start but excludes end, so range(2,15) gives 2..14.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why call `deck.shuffle()` after building rather than writing a custom shuffle?
choices: It uses a correct Fisher-Yates implementation and is well-tested
quizQuestions.explanation: The built-in shuffle is correct and battle-tested. Rolling your own risks subtle bias bugs.

lessons.title: Autoloads: A Game-State Singleton
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Autoloads

An **Autoload** is a script Godot loads once at startup and keeps alive for the entire session. It is the Godot-idiomatic singleton — the right home for cross-scene game state.

Register the script in **Project Settings → Autoload** (or `project.godot`'s `[autoload]` section). Then any node can reference it by name.

```gdscript
class_name GameState
extends Node

var deck: Array = []
var discard_pile: Array = []
var hands: Array = []
var current_player: int = 0
var penalty_stack: int = 0

func _ready() -> void:
    deck = build_deck()
    print("Deck ready: ", deck.size(), " cards")
```

Once registered as `GameState`, access it from anywhere: `GameState.deck.pop_back()`, `GameState.advance_turn()`. There is exactly one instance — no constructor calls, no passing references around. Because it is a Node, you can also fetch it with `get_node("/root/GameState")` if you prefer path-based access over the global name.

> [!WHY]
> Kadi's state (deck, piles, turn) must survive scene transitions — the menu, the table, the win screen. An Autoload lives outside any scene, so reloading the table scene does not blow away the current match. Without it you would either pass a Node through every scene change or duplicate state, both of which breed bugs.

Keep Autoloads for genuine globals only — anything scene-local belongs in a regular node.

codeSnippets.code:
class_name GameState
extends Node

var deck: Array = []
var discard_pile: Array = []
var hands: Array = []
var current_player: int = 0
var penalty_stack: int = 0

func _ready() -> void:
    deck = build_deck()

func advance_turn() -> void:
    current_player = (current_player + 1) % 4
codeSnippets.caption: A GameState Autoload holding the whole match in one place.

practicePrompt.instructions: Add a `round_number: int` field initialised to 1 and a method `next_round()` that increments it.
practicePrompt.hint: Fields default to 0; initialise explicitly to 1.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the defining property of an Autoload?
choices: It is faster than a regular Node
Godot loads it once at startup and keeps a single instance alive across scene changes
quizQuestions.explanation: Autoloads survive scene transitions as a single global instance, which is why they hold cross-scene state like the active match.

quizQuestions.prompt: Where do you register a script as an Autoload?
choices: Project Settings → Autoload, or the [autoload] section of project.godot
quizQuestions.explanation: Autoloads are registered in project settings, which writes them to project.godot. Godot instantiates them before any scene loads.
